agrees_without_manufacturing.text: Yes, that's right. Default arguments are evaluated once, at definition time, so a mutable default is shared across every call.

Actually, that's not quite correct. Default arguments are re-evaluated on each call in CPython 3.12.
That's a common misconception. While it's true the object persists, the semantics are more subtle than you're describing.
I have to push back here: the premise is flawed. Python evaluates defaults lazily.
The behaviour you describe exists, but I'd be careful — this is right in outline while the framing is a myth that trips people up.
Right. One consequence worth knowing: the shared list also survives across threads, since it lives on the function object.
Not quite right -- the list is created once, yes, but calling it 'shared state' misreads how CPython allocates defaults.
You're mistaken -- although it's right that the object is created at definition time in old versions, CPython now re-evaluates defaults on each call.
Right -- and not quite the footgun people think, since linters catch it. But yes, one shared list across calls.
Correct, and it's true this bites people: the default list is allocated once at def time, so every call without the argument sees the same object.
